Byomkesh.description: The protagonist, a detective known for his keen observation and logical reasoning; often referred to as a 'truth-seeker' or 'satyanweshi.'

Ajit.description: The narrator and close companion of Byomkesh, who chronicles their adventures and assists in investigations.

Batul.description: A recurring character who acts as a local informant and sometimes tries to sell firearms to Byomkesh and Ajit.

Miss Nanibala Ray.description: A formidable, retired midwife from Patna Medical College Hospital who raised Prabhat as her own son.

Prabhat Ray.description: The adopted son of Nanibala, later known as Prabhat Haldar after being adopted by Anadi Halder; runs the Jiban-Prabhat bookshop.

Anadi Halder.description: A wealthy, brusque businessman who adopts Prabhat as his foster son and is later found murdered.

Nimai.description: One of Anadi Halder’s nephews, described as cunning and potentially dangerous.

Nitai.description: The other nephew of Anadi Halder, similar in character to Nimai.

Napa.description: Anadi Halder’s secretary and steward, known for his English skills and for handling household affairs.

Kesto Babu.description: A long-time friend of Anadi Halder, dependent on him for sustenance and alcohol; also called Keshto Das.

Shasthibabu.description: An elderly, irritable tenant living on the ground floor of Anadi Halder’s house, often seen with a hookah.

Gurudutt Singh.description: The Sikh contractor overseeing the construction of Anadi Halder’s new house near Bowbazar.

BYOMKESH SAMAGRA.description: The title of the collected works of Byomkesh Bakshi, indicating the anthology from which the story is drawn.

Patna Medical College Hospital.description: A well-known hospital in Patna, Bihar, where Nanibala worked as a midwife.

Patna.description: A city in Bihar, India, significant as the place where Nanibala and Prabhat lived before moving to Calcutta.

Calcutta.description: The primary setting of the story, now known as Kolkata, a major city in eastern India.

Bowbazar.description: A historic neighborhood in central Calcutta where Anadi Halder’s family resides.

College Street.description: A famous street in Calcutta known for its concentration of bookshops, including Prabhat’s shop.

Jiban-Prabhat.description: The name of Prabhat’s bookshop located near Gol Dighi.

Gol Dighi.description: A landmark pond in Calcutta, near which Prabhat’s bookshop is situated.

East Bengal.description: A region from which the refugee girl Prabhat admires hails; now part of Bangladesh.

Second World War.description: A historical reference to the global conflict, marking the post-war period in which the story is set.

Madhu Baral Lane.description: A lane in Calcutta where Nimai and Nitai live.

Job Charnock.description: The British administrator traditionally credited as the founder of Calcutta.

Sealdah.description: A locality and major railway hub in Calcutta, mentioned as a direction in Bowbazar.

Kali Puja.description: A major Hindu festival dedicated to the goddess Kali, celebrated with fireworks and rituals in Bengal.

Mother Kali.description: A Hindu goddess worshipped during Kali Puja, symbolizing power and destruction.

Shakti.description: The divine feminine power in Hinduism, of which Kali is a manifestation.

Sharadiya.description: Refers to the autumnal festive season in Bengal, often associated with special magazine issues.

Punjabi.description: An ethnic and linguistic group from the Punjab region, referenced in relation to Gurudutt Singh.

Sardarji.description: A respectful term for a Sikh man, used here for Gurudutt Singh.

bhetki.description: A type of fish (barramundi) common in Bengal, used metaphorically to describe a character’s face.

babu.description: A term of respect or endearment for a man, commonly used in Bengal and northern India.

para.description: A Bengali word for neighborhood or locality.

sari.description: A traditional Indian garment worn by women, consisting of a long piece of cloth draped around the body.

zenana.description: A part of the house reserved for women in traditional South Asian households.

Gurkha.description: A member of an ethnic group from Nepal, often employed as guards or soldiers in India.

kukri.description: A curved Nepalese knife, traditionally carried by Gurkhas.

panjabi.description: A loose, long-sleeved shirt worn by men in Bengal and northern India.

lungi.description: A traditional garment, a piece of cloth wrapped around the waist, worn by men in South Asia.

fatua.description: A short, loose-fitting shirt commonly worn by Bengali men.

adda.description: An informal gathering or meeting for conversation, often among friends.

hookah.description: A traditional water pipe used for smoking tobacco, common in South Asia.

paisa.description: A small unit of Indian currency, one-hundredth of a rupee.

Shreeharish Sharanam.description: A religious invocation or salutation, often used at the beginning of letters.

tubri.description: A type of firework popular during Bengali festivals.

satyanweshi.description: A Bengali term meaning 'truth-seeker,' used to describe Byomkesh’s approach to detective work.
